questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases
questions.stem: The left panel illustrates molecular mimicry, in which a T-cell receptor reacts with a self-peptide that shares structural homology with a microbial antigen. Cross-reactivity between streptococcal M protein and cardiac tissue by this mechanism causes which disease?

explanation.summary: In molecular mimicry, antibodies or T cells raised against a pathogen cross-react with structurally similar self-antigens. Antibodies against group A streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve tissue, producing rheumatic fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: In molecular mimicry, antibodies or T cells raised against a pathogen cross-react with structurally similar self-antigens. Antibodies against group A streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve tissue, producing rheumatic fever.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases
questions.stem: In this sequence an infected cell is damaged and leaks self-antigens, which antigen-presenting cells then present to autoreactive T cells, ultimately driving immune responses against uninfected cells. What best explains why the response broadens to target uninfected host cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tissue damage releases previously sequestered self-antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pathogen directly infects all host cells simultaneously

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thymus begins producing new self-reactive clones on demand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autoantibodies are transferred from the mother

explanation.summary: This is epitope spreading: cell injury during infection releases hidden self-antigens that are taken up and presented, activating autoreactive lymphocytes. The immune response then expands beyond the original microbial target to self-tissues, contributing to autoimmune disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is epitope spreading: cell injury during infection releases hidden self-antigens that are taken up and presented, activating autoreactive lymphocytes. The immune response then expands beyond the original microbial target to self-tissues, contributing to autoimmune disease.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases
questions.stem: This crystal structure shows an antigenic peptide bound in the groove of an HLA-DR molecule and contacted by a T-cell receptor. HLA-DR is a class II MHC molecule; it presents peptides to which cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B cells via their B-cell receptor

explanation.summary: HLA-DR, -DP, and -DQ are MHC class II molecules expressed on professional antigen-presenting cells. They present exogenously derived peptides to CD4+ helper T cells, whose TCR, together with the CD4 co-receptor binding MHC II, recognizes the peptide-MHC complex.
explanation.whyCorrect: HLA-DR, -DP, and -DQ are MHC class II molecules expressed on professional antigen-presenting cells. They present exogenously derived peptides to CD4+ helper T cells, whose TCR, together with the CD4 co-receptor binding MHC II, recognizes the peptide-MHC complex.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases
questions.stem: This spectrum ranges from autoinflammatory disorders (e.g., familial Mediterranean fever, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome) at one end to autoimmune disorders (e.g., SLE, myasthenia gravis) at the other. Diseases at the autoinflammatory end are driven primarily by which arm of the immune system?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The adaptive immune system (autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells)

explanation.summary: Autoinflammatory disorders arise from dysregulated innate immunity (e.g., inflammasome/IL-1 overactivation) without autoantibodies or antigen-specific T cells, causing recurrent unprovoked inflammation. Autoimmune disorders at the other end involve the adaptive system, with autoreactive T cells and autoantibodies against specific self-antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoinflammatory disorders arise from dysregulated innate immunity (e.g., inflammasome/IL-1 overactivation) without autoantibodies or antigen-specific T cells, causing recurrent unprovoked inflammation. Autoimmune disorders at the other end involve the adaptive system, with autoreactive T cells and autoantibodies against specific self-antigens.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Autoinflammatory and Autoimmune Diseases
questions.stem: This figure shows central tolerance, including deletion of self-reactive T cells in the thymus. Failure of thymic negative selection due to a defect in the AIRE gene results in what?

explanation.summary: AIRE (autoimmune regulator) drives thymic expression of peripheral self-antigens so self-reactive T cells are deleted (central tolerance). AIRE mutations impair this negative selection, allowing autoreactive T cells to escape and cause autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy (APECED).
explanation.whyCorrect: AIRE (autoimmune regulator) drives thymic expression of peripheral self-antigens so self-reactive T cells are deleted (central tolerance). AIRE mutations impair this negative selection, allowing autoreactive T cells to escape and cause autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy (APECED).

questions.stem: The left panel shows a CD8+ T cell killing a cancer cell; the right shows the same tumor cell (now poorly presenting antigen on MHC I) killed by a different lymphocyte. Why can the right-hand lymphocyte kill the tumor when the CD8+ T cell cannot?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NK cells must first be primed by dendritic cells in lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: NK cells preferentially lyse cells that overexpress MHC class I

choices.label: C
choices.text: NK cells recognize peptide-MHC through a rearranged T-cell receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: NK cells are activated by loss of inhibitory MHC class I

choices.label: E
choices.text: NK cells kill only after antibody opsonization via CD16

explanation.summary: Tumor or viral downregulation of MHC I lets cells evade CD8+ T cells but simultaneously removes the inhibitory signal to NK cells. Reduced 'self' MHC together with activating-ligand engagement and cytokines triggers NK-mediated perforin/granzyme killing (the missing-self hypothesis).
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor or viral downregulation of MHC I lets cells evade CD8+ T cells but simultaneously removes the inhibitory signal to NK cells. Reduced 'self' MHC together with activating-ligand engagement and cytokines triggers NK-mediated perforin/granzyme killing (the missing-self hypothesis).

questions.stem: One tumor immune-escape mechanism shown is loss of MHC class I so cytotoxic T lymphocytes can no longer recognize the tumor. Which effector cell is best positioned to eliminate such MHC-I-deficient tumor cells?

explanation.summary: Downregulating MHC I evades CTLs but sensitizes the tumor to NK cells, which kill targets lacking inhibitory MHC I. Other escape strategies depicted include tolerization by APCs, antigen modulation, secretion of TGF-beta/IL-10, and creation of an immune-privileged barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Downregulating MHC I evades CTLs but sensitizes the tumor to NK cells, which kill targets lacking inhibitory MHC I. Other escape strategies depicted include tolerization by APCs, antigen modulation, secretion of TGF-beta/IL-10, and creation of an immune-privileged barrier.

questions.stem: This figure shows preformed circulating recipient antibodies binding donor (allogeneic) HLA on graft endothelium within minutes to hours, activating complement and damaging endothelium. Which pre-transplant test detects these preformed antibodies and prevents this reaction?

explanation.summary: Hyperacute rejection is mediated by preformed recipient antibodies against donor HLA or ABO antigens, causing immediate complement activation, thrombosis, and endothelial injury. A pre-transplant crossmatch (mixing recipient serum with donor lymphocytes) detects such antibodies so incompatible grafts are avoided.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperacute rejection is mediated by preformed recipient antibodies against donor HLA or ABO antigens, causing immediate complement activation, thrombosis, and endothelial injury. A pre-transplant crossmatch (mixing recipient serum with donor lymphocytes) detects such antibodies so incompatible grafts are avoided.

questions.stem: These plots show sequence variability across the MHC class I and class II molecules. Where is the polymorphism (sequence variability) concentrated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the residues lining the peptide-binding groove

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evenly distributed along the entire molecule

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the invariant beta-2 microglobulin domain

explanation.summary: MHC polymorphism clusters in the peptide-binding cleft (alpha-1/alpha-2 for class I; alpha-1/beta-1 for class II), diversifying the repertoire of peptides presented across a population. Framework and membrane-proximal domains such as beta-2 microglobulin are conserved.
explanation.whyCorrect: MHC polymorphism clusters in the peptide-binding cleft (alpha-1/alpha-2 for class I; alpha-1/beta-1 for class II), diversifying the repertoire of peptides presented across a population. Framework and membrane-proximal domains such as beta-2 microglobulin are conserved.

questions.stem: This figure depicts a rejection developing over days to weeks, featuring recipient CD8+ T cells attacking graft parenchymal cells and endothelium (endothelialitis). Compared with hyperacute rejection, what is the principal mechanism of this (acute) rejection?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrosis and vascular narrowing developing over years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preformed recipient antibodies present before transplant

explanation.summary: Acute rejection occurs days to weeks after transplantation and is driven chiefly by recipient T cells (notably CD8+ cytotoxic T cells) recognizing donor HLA, with a variable antibody-mediated component (endothelialitis). It is distinct from antibody-driven hyperacute rejection (minutes-hours) and chronic rejection (months-years).
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute rejection occurs days to weeks after transplantation and is driven chiefly by recipient T cells (notably CD8+ cytotoxic T cells) recognizing donor HLA, with a variable antibody-mediated component (endothelialitis). It is distinct from antibody-driven hyperacute rejection (minutes-hours) and chronic rejection (months-years).

questions.stem: This process, developing over months to years after solid-organ transplantation, is illustrated. What is the characteristic vascular lesion responsible for graft failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granulomatous destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutrophilic fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls within minutes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Massive interstitial hemorrhage from platelet thrombi

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complement-mediated lysis of graft endothelium by preformed antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Concentric intimal smooth-muscle proliferation causing vessel occlusion

explanation.summary: Chronic rejection is driven by recipient CD4+ T cells and macrophages responding to graft alloantigens, secreting cytokines that stimulate intimal smooth-muscle proliferation and fibrosis, progressively occluding vessels over months to years. Hyperacute rejection (preformed antibodies) occurs in minutes and acute rejection over days to weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rejection is driven by recipient CD4+ T cells and macrophages responding to graft alloantigens, secreting cytokines that stimulate intimal smooth-muscle proliferation and fibrosis, progressively occluding vessels over months to years. Hyperacute rejection (preformed antibodies) occurs in minutes and acute rejection over days to weeks.

questions.stem: A naive strain B mouse rejects a strain A skin graft in 14 days; a second strain A graft placed later is rejected in only 6 days. What accounts for the accelerated second-set rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Innate complement activation triggered by the second graft

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of MHC expression on the second graft

explanation.summary: Second-set rejection is faster and more vigorous because the first exposure generated antigen-specific memory T lymphocytes against strain A alloantigens. Specificity and memory are defining features of the adaptive immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Second-set rejection is faster and more vigorous because the first exposure generated antigen-specific memory T lymphocytes against strain A alloantigens. Specificity and memory are defining features of the adaptive immune response.
